content: Airborne dust originating from outside the home can contribute to lead exposure. The lead content in dust collected from floors, windowsills, and window wells has been shown to correlate with blood lead levels (BLLs) in children. A recent analysis of data from 12 studies involving children aged 6 to 36 months demonstrated a strong direct relationship between the amount of lead in dust and the risk of elevated blood lead levels (EBLLs). This association was observed even at dust lead levels below the 40 µg/ft² threshold for lead hazards in floor dust, as defined by the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD) and the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA). For windowsills, lead levels of 250 µg/ft² are considered hazardous. Soil and exterior dust contamination have been linked to point-source emissions, such as lead smelters, historical use of leaded gasoline, and the weathering of exterior lead-based paint. Soil near homes typically contains higher lead levels than soil from other areas of the yard. Hazardous levels of lead in soil are not uncommon. A national survey found that homes with intact exterior lead-based paint are over three times more likely to have soil lead levels exceeding 500 ppm compared to homes without exterior lead paint (21% vs. 6%). Additionally, soil contamination is eight times more common at homes with deteriorated exterior lead-based paint compared to homes without lead paint (48% vs. 6%). In urban areas, high lead levels have also been detected in exterior dust collected from paved surfaces, such as sidewalks. Soil lead content is a significant predictor of children’s risk for EBLLs, though it is less influential than the lead content of interior floor dust. Soil samples from play areas in yards show a stronger relationship to children’s BLLs than samples from other locations. The EPA defines a soil lead hazard as bare soil containing 400 ppm of lead in play areas or 1,200 ppm in other parts of a yard. Lead in tap water typically originates from the corrosion of lead-containing materials in water distribution systems and household plumbing. Exposure to lead in tap water has been reduced over the past two decades due to measures implemented under the 1986 and 1996 amendments to the Safe Drinking Water Act and the EPA’s Lead and Copper Rule. This regulation requires public water systems to monitor lead levels in tap water and take action if lead concentrations exceed 15 µg/L in more than 10% of household samples. Actions include public education, water treatment to reduce corrosivity, and, in some cases, replacement of lead service lines. However, these regulations do not apply to the over 40 million households relying on private well water, which can have elevated lead levels if the water is corrosive and lead is present in the well pump or plumbing. Most jurisdictions do not monitor lead levels in private well water. Studies, primarily involving adults, suggest that exposure to water with lead levels near the EPA action level is unlikely to cause EBLLs on its own. However, individual risk varies based on circumstances and water consumption. For example, infants consuming formula prepared with lead-contaminated water may be at higher risk due to their high water intake relative to body size. Interventions to reduce residential lead exposure include addressing immediate hazards, such as removing or covering deteriorated lead-based paint, repairing or replacing windows to prevent lead paint abrasion, sealing floors to create smooth and cleanable surfaces, using professional cleaners to control household dust, and covering bare, contaminated soil. Additional measures may prevent future lead hazards, such as replacing building components with lead-based paint (intact or not) and stripping lead paint from components left in the home. Most studies evaluating the effectiveness of lead hazard control measures in reducing EBLLs lack controls and were conducted before stringent procedures to limit lead dust contamination were established. Earlier studies showed that among children with baseline BLLs above 25 µg/dL, interventions to remove or repair deteriorated lead-based paint resulted in BLL reductions of 20% to 30% over the following year. In one controlled study, children in treated homes experienced BLL declines approximately twice as large as those in untreated homes. However, extensive removal of lead-based paint without measures to prevent exposure to abatement dust and debris has been associated with increases in children’s BLLs, likely due to elevated lead levels in house dust. Consequently, many jurisdictions now prohibit hazardous paint removal methods, such as uncontained power sanding, and require safe work practices, cleaning, and dust lead testing to protect occupants. Post-intervention dust lead levels must meet clearance standards before reoccupancy. Clearance standards for public and federally assisted housing are 40 µg/ft² for floors, 250 µg/ft² for windowsills, and 400 µg/ft² for window wells. Some state and local jurisdictions have established different clearance standards.
